Proverb: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush' means that it's better to hold onto something you have rather than take the risk of getting something better which may come to nothing.

Proverb: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step' puts forward the notion that, however difficult a task is, you can only complete it if you first start it.

Proverb: A leopard cannot change its spots
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'A leopard cannot change its spots' expresses the notion that things cannot change their innate nature. It is normally used to suggest that people who have done bad things will always be bad people.

Proverb: A little knowledge is a dangerous thing
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'A little knowledge is a dangerous thing' expresses the idea that a small amount of knowledge can mislead people into thinking that they are more expert than they really are, which can lead to mistakes being made.

Proverb: A rolling stone gathers no moss
Correct_Meaning: Someone who does not settle in one place rarely prospers.

Proverb: A stitch in time saves nine
Correct_Meaning: A 'stitch in time' is a timely effort that will prevent more work later.

Proverb: A watched pot never boils
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial expression 'a watched pot never boils' refers to the feeling time seems to go slower when you are anxiously waiting for something to happen.

Proverb: A wolf in sheep's clothing
Correct_Meaning: A wolf in sheep's clothing' is someone who hides malicious intent under the guise of kindliness.

Proverb: Absolute power corrupts absolutely
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'power corrupts; absolute power corrupts absolutely' conveys the opinion that, as a person's power increases, their moral sense diminishes.

Proverb: Actions speak louder than words
Correct_Meaning: This proverb express the idea that a person's actions are a better indication of their character than what he or she says.

Proverb: All that glitters is not gold / All that glisters is not gold
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'All that glitters is not gold' means that not everything that is shiny and superficially attractive is valuable.

Proverb: All things come to those who wait
Correct_Meaning: A literal meaning, advocating patience.

Proverb: All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy' expresses the idea that working constantly and making no time for enjoyment makes one bored and boring.

Proverb: An apple a day keeps the doctor away
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'An apple a day keeps the doctor away' has a straightforward literal, and very probably correct, meaning - that the eating of fruit maintains good health.

Proverb: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth' expresses the notion that for every wrong done there should be a compensating measure of justice.

Proverb: Barking up the wrong tree
Correct_Meaning: Making a mistake or a false assumption in something you are trying to achieve.

Proverb: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder
Correct_Meaning: Beauty in the eye of the beholder' has a literal meaning - that the perception of beauty is subjective - what one person finds beautiful another may not.

Proverb: Beggars can't be choosers
Correct_Meaning: If you request something to be given you should not question what you are given.

Proverb: Beware of Greeks bearing gifts
Correct_Meaning: Don't trust your enemies.

Proverb: Big fleas have little fleas upon their back to bite 'em
Correct_Meaning: Everyone is preyed upon by someone, who in turn has someone preying on them.

Proverb: Birds of a feather flock together
Correct_Meaning: Those of similar taste congregate in groups.

Proverb: Blood is thicker than water
Correct_Meaning: By saying 'blood is thicker than water' we mean that family bonds are closer than those of outsiders.

Proverb: Bolt from the blue
Correct_Meaning: A complete surprise, like a bolt of lightning from a clear blue sky.

Proverb: Born with a silver spoon in one's mouth
Correct_Meaning: To be born with a silver spoon in one's mouth is to be born into a wealthy and privileged family.

Proverb: Boys will be boys
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'boys will be boys' is used to express resignation at, or even encouragement of, the bad behaviour of boys, imagining it to be an inevitable consequence of their gender.

Proverb: Bread always falls buttered side down
Correct_Meaning: The 'buttered side down' view of life is one that is pessimistic and fatalistic.

Proverb: Buck stops here - The
Correct_Meaning: The slogan 'The buck stops here' is a promise that responsibility will not be passed on to anyone else.

Proverb: Build a better mousetrap and the world will beat a path to your door
Correct_Meaning: To 'build a better mousetrap' is to make an improvement to an existing product or service. It especially refers to simple and straightforward changes that are obvious advances on earlier devices.

Proverb: Burn the candle at both ends
Correct_Meaning: To live at a hectic pace.

Proverb: Burning the midnight oil
Correct_Meaning: To 'burn the midnight oil' is to work late into the night. Originally this was by the light of an oil lamp or candle. More recently, the phrase is used figuratively, alluding back its use before electric lighting.

Proverb: Bury the hatchet
Correct_Meaning: To bury the hatchett is to settle your differences with an adversary.

Proverb: Bury your head in the sand
Correct_Meaning: Refuse to confront or acknowledge a problem.

Proverb: Butter no parsnips - Fine words
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'Fine words butter no parsnips' means that nothing concrete is achieved by empty words or flattery.

Proverb: By hook or by crook
Correct_Meaning: To do something 'by hook or by crook' is to do it by whatever means are necessary - be they fair or foul.

Proverb: By the skin of your teeth
Correct_Meaning: Narrowly; barely. Usually used in regard to a narrow escape from a disaster.

Proverb: Bygones be bygones - Let
Correct_Meaning: To 'let bygones be bygones' is to allow the unpleasant things that have happened in the past be forgotten.

Proverb: Call a spade a spade
Correct_Meaning: To call a spade a spade is to speak plainly - to describe something as it really is.

Proverb: Can't hold a candle to
Correct_Meaning: The expression 'can't hold a candle to' refers to someone who compares badly to an known authority - to be unfit even to hold a subordinate position.

Proverb: Carry coals to Newcastle
Correct_Meaning: To do something pointless and superfluous.

Proverb: Cart before the horse - Put the
Correct_Meaning: Reverse the accepted or logical order of things.

Proverb: Cast the first stone
Correct_Meaning: Be the first to attack a sinner. The implication in Jesus' teaching was that the members of the congregation were only in a position to condemn a sinner if they were without sin themselves - in other words, 'judge not lest you be judged'.

Proverb: Cat may look at a king - A
Correct_Meaning: An inferior isn't completely restricted in what they may do in the presence of a superior.

Proverb: Cat out of the bag - Let the
Correct_Meaning: To let the cat out of the bag is to disclose a secret, either deliberately or inadvertently.

Proverb: Chain is only as strong as its weakest link - A
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'A chain is only as strong as its weakest link' has a literal meaning, although the 'weakest link' referred to is figurative and usually applies to a person or technical feature rather than the link of an actual chain.

Proverb: Charity begins at home
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'charity begins at home' expresses the overriding demand to take care of one's family, before caring for others.

Proverb: Chickens come home to roost
Correct_Meaning: Bad deeds or words return to discomfort their perpetrator.

Proverb: Cleanliness is next to godliness
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'cleanliness is next to godliness' expresses the idea that those who are pure and wholesome are close to God.

Proverb: Close, but no cigar
Correct_Meaning: The expression 'close but no cigar' is used to indicate that someone has fallen just short of a successful outcome and failed to secure any reward.

Proverb: Clutch at straws
Correct_Meaning: Try any route to get out of a desperate situation, no matter how unlikely it is to succeed.

Proverb: Cock and bull story
Correct_Meaning: A fanciful and unbelievable tale.

Proverb: Cold feet
Correct_Meaning: To 'get cold feet' is to become disheartened or timid, losing one's previous enthusiasm or courage.

Proverb: Come clean
Correct_Meaning: To make a full disclosure; to confess.

Proverb: Come up trumps
Correct_Meaning: To complete something well or successfully, especially in circumstances in which it isn't expected.

Proverb: Come what come may
Correct_Meaning: Let whatever events crop up come to pass.

Proverb: Cool as a cucumber
Correct_Meaning: As cool as a cucumber' means calm and unruffled.

Proverb: Cost an arm and a leg
Correct_Meaning: A large, possibly exorbitant, amount of money.

Proverb: Count your chickens before they are hatched
Correct_Meaning: Don't be hasty in evaluating one's assets.

Proverb: Crocodile tears
Correct_Meaning: To weep crocodile tears is to put on an insincere show of sorrow.

Proverb: Curate's egg
Correct_Meaning: Something bad that is called good out of politeness or timidity.

Proverb: Curiosity killed the cat
Correct_Meaning: Inquisitiveness can lead one into dangerous situations.

Proverb: Customer is always right - The
Correct_Meaning: The customer is always right' is a trading slogan that states a company's keenness to be seen to put the customer first. The implied suggestion is that the company is so customer focussed that they will say the customer is right, even if they aren't.

Proverb: Cut off your nose to spite your face
Correct_Meaning: To 'cut off your nose to spite your face' is to disadvantage yourself in order to do harm to an adversary.

Proverb: Daniel come to judgement
Correct_Meaning: Someone who makes a wise judgement about something that has previously proven difficult to resolve.

Proverb: Dark horse
Correct_Meaning: A dark horse is someone, who was previously little known, emerges to prominence in a competition.

Proverb: Darkest hour - The
Correct_Meaning: The darkest hour is the time when bad events are at their worst and most dispiriting.

Proverb: Darkest hour is just before the dawn - The
Correct_Meaning: There is hope, even in the worst of circumstances.

Proverb: Dead as a dodo
Correct_Meaning: Unambiguously and unequivocally dead.

Proverb: Dead as a doornail
Correct_Meaning: To be 'as dead as a doornail' is to be utterly dead, devoid of life (when applied to people, plants or animals) or finished with, unusable (when applied to inanimate objects).

Proverb: Dead in the water
Correct_Meaning: A dead in the water ship is one that is motionless and without power. The figurative expression 'dead in the water' means 'unable to function; without hope of future success; doomed'.

Proverb: Devil and the deep blue sea
Correct_Meaning: In difficulty, faced with two dangerous alternatives.

Proverb: Devil take the hindmost - The
Correct_Meaning: A proverbial phrase indicating that those who lag behind will receive no aid.

Proverb: Diamond in the rough
Correct_Meaning: Someone who is basically good hearted but lacking social graces and respect for the law.

Proverb: Die has been cast - The
Correct_Meaning: The die has been cast' means that an irrevocable choice has been made.

Proverb: Different kettle of fish
Correct_Meaning: A different kettle of fish' is an alternative to what has been previously considered; a different thing altogether.

Proverb: Dish fit for the gods - A
Correct_Meaning: An offering of high quality.

Proverb: Dog in the manger
Correct_Meaning: Spiteful and mean-spirited.

Proverb: Dog is a man's best friend
Correct_Meaning: An animal that performs valuable service to humans, often with reference to dogs.

Proverb: Dollars to doughnuts
Correct_Meaning: An outcome that is almost assured; a certainty.

Proverb: Donkey's years
Correct_Meaning: A very long time.

Proverb: Don't cast your pearls before swine
Correct_Meaning: Items of quality offered to those who aren't cultured enough to appreciate them.

Proverb: Don't change horses in midstream
Correct_Meaning: Don't change your leader or your basic position when part-way through a campaign or a project .

Proverb: Don't keep a dog and bark yourself
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'don't keep a dog and bark yourself' is advice that you should not pay someone to do a task and then do it yourself.

Proverb: Don't look a gift horse in the mouth
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'don't look a gift horse in the mouth' means don't be ungrateful when you receive a gift.

Proverb: Don't shut the stable door after the horse has bolted
Correct_Meaning: Don't waste time taking precautions when the damage has already been done.

Proverb: Don't throw good money after bad
Correct_Meaning: You 'throw good money after bad' when, following the loss of some money, you to incur a further loss in trying to make good.

Proverb: Don't throw the baby out with the bathwater
Correct_Meaning: Don't discard something valuable along with something undesirable.

Proverb: Don't try to teach your Grandma to suck eggs
Correct_Meaning: Don't offer advice to someone who has more experience than oneself.

Proverb: Drop in the bucket - A
Correct_Meaning: A drop in the bucket is a very small and insignificant proportion of the whole.

Proverb: Early bird catches the worm - The
Correct_Meaning: Success comes to those who prepare well and put in effort.

Proverb: East, west, home's best
Correct_Meaning: This proverbial saying express the idea that, wherever you travel in the world, your home is the best place to be.

Proverb: Eat humble pie
Correct_Meaning: Act submissively and apologetically, especially in admitting an error.

Proverb: Elephant in the room
Correct_Meaning: An important and obvious topic, which everyone present is aware of, but which isn't discussed, as such discussion is considered to be uncomfortable.

Proverb: Emperor's new clothes
Correct_Meaning: The label given to any fictional item that viewers have been induced into believing as real..

Proverb: Enough is as good as a feast
Correct_Meaning: To get Enough is enough is to come off worst in a bargain or contest.

Proverb: Englishman's home is his castle
Correct_Meaning: The English dictum that a man's home is his refuge.

Proverb: Every cloud has a silver lining
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'every cloud has a silver lining' is used to convey the notion that, no matter how bad a situation might seem, there is always has some good aspect to it.

Proverb: Exception that proves the rule - The
Correct_Meaning: Normally with these meanings and origins the meaning is well-understood or self-evident and the interesting aspect is how, where and when the phrase originated. This one is a little different - it's the meaning that is generally not understood.

Proverb: Face the music
Correct_Meaning: Accept the unpleasant consequences of one's actions.

Proverb: Fair exchange is no robbery
Correct_Meaning: An exchange of two things of equal value is a reasonable and honest trade.

Proverb: Faith will move mountains
Correct_Meaning: Faith is immensely powerful.

Proverb: Fall on your sword
Correct_Meaning: To 'fall on your sword' is, literally, to commit suicide or, figuratively, to offer your resignation.

Proverb: Feather in one's cap - A
Correct_Meaning: A symbol of honour and achievement.

Proverb: Fiddling while Rome burns
Correct_Meaning: To occupy oneself with unimportant matters and neglect priorities during a crisis.

Proverb: Fight fire with fire
Correct_Meaning: Respond to an attack by using a similar method as one's attacker.

Proverb: Fish rot from the head down
Correct_Meaning: When an organization or state fails, it is the leadership that is the root cause.

Proverb: Fish or cut bait
Correct_Meaning: There is some uncertainty about the precise meaning of this phrase. Some use it to mean 'make a choice about what you intend to do'; others have it that it means 'either get to work in a productive manner or do something else and let someone else work'. The second meaning, which I favour, and which is more common, is similar in meaning to 'put up or shut up', or the 20th century US vulgarism 'shit or get off the pot'.

Proverb: Fish out of water - A
Correct_Meaning: Someone who is in a situation they are unsuited to.

Proverb: Flash in the pan
Correct_Meaning: Something which disappoints by failing to deliver anything of value, despite a showy beginning.

Proverb: Flogging a dead horse
Correct_Meaning: To flog a dead horse is to attempt to revive an interest which has died out; to engage in fruitless effort.

Proverb: Fly by the seat of one's pants
Correct_Meaning: To 'fly by the seat of your pants' is to decide a course of action as you go along, using your own initiative and perceptions rather than a predetermined plan or mechanical aids.

Proverb: Fly in the ointment
Correct_Meaning: A fly in the ointment is a small but irritating flaw that spoils the whole. In the 20th century the expression has also come to be used to describe a small flaw that comes to light to spoil an otherwise faultless plan.

Proverb: Fools rush in where angels fear to tread
Correct_Meaning: The rash or inexperienced will attempt things that wiser people are more cautious of.

Proverb: Fool's errand
Correct_Meaning: A pointless undertaking.

Proverb: Fool's paradise - A
Correct_Meaning: A state of happiness based on false hope.

Proverb: Foot in the door - A
Correct_Meaning: An introduction or way in to something, made in order that progress may be made later.

Proverb: For all intents and purposes
Correct_Meaning: In effect; for all practical purposes.

Proverb: For every thing there is a season
Correct_Meaning: There is an appropriate time for everything.

Proverb: Foregone conclusion
Correct_Meaning: A decision made before the evidence for it is known. An inevitable conclusion.

Proverb: Forewarned is forearmed
Correct_Meaning: Advance warning provides an advantage.

Proverb: From strength to strength
Correct_Meaning: Progress from one success to another higher level of success.

Proverb: Genius is one percent inspiration and 99 percent perspiration
Correct_Meaning: Genius is largely the result of hard work, rather than an inspired flash of insight.

Proverb: Get down to brass tacks
Correct_Meaning: Engage with the basic facts or realities.

Proverb: Gild the lily
Correct_Meaning: To apply unnecessary ornament - to over embellish.

Proverb: Give a man a fish and you will feed him for a day
Correct_Meaning: This proverbial saying suggests that the ability to work is of greater benefit than a one-off handout.

Proverb: Go by the book
Correct_Meaning: Correctly; according to the rules.

Proverb: Go off half-cocked
Correct_Meaning: Speak or act prematurely.

Proverb: Go out on a limb
Correct_Meaning: Put oneself in an isolated position in one's support of someone or something.

Proverb: Go the whole hog
Correct_Meaning: To perform some act or adopt some opinion fully and thoroughly.

Proverb: Golden key can open any door - A
Correct_Meaning: A golden key opens any door' is the opinion that sufficient money, or the promise of it, will allow the possessor of it to do anything they wish.

Proverb: grain of salt
Correct_Meaning: To take a statement with 'a grain of salt' (or 'a pinch of salt') means to accept it while maintaining a degree of scepticism about its truth.

Proverb: Grasp the nettle
Correct_Meaning: To tackle a difficult problem boldly.

Proverb: Great minds think alike
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'great minds think alike' has a straightforward literal meaning. However, the usage is often ironic, that is, it is used when two unexceptional minds have the same thought.

Proverb: Grist to the mill
Correct_Meaning: All things are a potential source of profit or advantage.

Proverb: Half a loaf is better than no bread
Correct_Meaning: Something, even if it isn't what you ideally would prefer, is better than nothing.

Proverb: Handle with kid gloves
Correct_Meaning: Handle a situation, or a person or an object, delicately and gingerly.

Proverb: Hard and fast
Correct_Meaning: Rigidly adhered to - without doubt or debate.

Proverb: Hard cases make bad law
Correct_Meaning: Hard', that is, exceptional, legal cases aren't suitable as the source of generalised laws.

Proverb: Haste makes waste
Correct_Meaning: Rushing into a decision may cause mistakes that waste more time than would have been taken by proceeding more carefully.

Proverb: Have an axe to grind
Correct_Meaning: To have an axe to grind is to have a dispute to take up with someone or, to have an ulterior motive; to have private ends to serve.

Proverb: He who laughs last laughs longest
Correct_Meaning: See also: the List of Proverbs.

Proverb: He who sups with the devil should have a long spoon
Correct_Meaning: This proverbial saying suggests that, if you have dealings with wicked people you should be cautious and distance yourself from them, or else you may be corrupted into their evil ways.

Proverb: Hedge your bets
Correct_Meaning: To avoid committing oneself; to leave a means of retreat open.

Proverb: Hell has no fury like a woman scorned
Correct_Meaning: Hell has no fury like a woman scorned' conveys the idea that a scorned woman (that is, one who has been betrayed) is more furious than anything that hell can devise.

Proverb: Here lies one whose name is writ in water
Correct_Meaning: Fame, and indeed life, is fleeting.

Proverb: Home is where the heart is
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'home is where the heart is' means that, wherever you are and whoever you are with, your home and family provide the greatest emotional bond.

Proverb: Honesty is the best policy
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'Honesty is the best policy' has a straightforward literal meaning, which encourages the populace to tell the turth and avoid crime.

Proverb: Honey catches more flies than vinegar
Correct_Meaning: This proverbial saying expresses the idea that it is more effective to be polite and ingratiating than to be hostile or demanding.

Proverb: Horse-sense
Correct_Meaning: A robust form of common sense believed to be found in poorly educated but shrewd people.

Proverb: If the mountain will not come to Muhammad, then Muhammad must go to the mountain
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial phrase 'If the mountain will not come to Muhammad...' means that , if one's will does not prevail, one must submit to an alternative.

Proverb: If you can't stand the heat, get out of the kitchen
Correct_Meaning: Don't persist with a task if the pressure of it is too much for you. The implication being that, if you can't cope, you should leave the work to someone who can.

Proverb: If you think that, you have another think coming
Correct_Meaning: To have 'another think coming' is to be greatly mistaken. The phrase is usually spoken by an antagonist as 'you have another think coming'; the implication being that one will shortly be obliged to adopt a different viewpoint, either by the presentation of indisputable evidence, or by force.

Proverb: It's better to give than to receive
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'It's better to give than to receive' has a straightforward literal meaning which needs no further explanation.

Proverb: It's better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'It's better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all' has a straightforward literal meaning.

Proverb: Necessity is the mother of invention
Correct_Meaning: Difficult situations inspire ingenious solutions.

Proverb: Nothing is certain but death and taxes
Correct_Meaning: A rather fatalistic and sardonic proverb. It draws on the actual inevitability of death to highlight the difficulty in avoiding the burden of taxes.

Proverb: Nothing succeeds like success
Correct_Meaning: A proverb, expressing the idea that success breeds further success.

Proverb: Nothing ventured, nothing gained
Correct_Meaning: In order to achieve, you need to act and take risks.

Proverb: Once bitten, twice shy
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'once bitten, twice shy' suggests that, when someone is hurt doing something, they are wary of doing it again for fear of being hurt a second time.

Proverb: One-hit wonder
Correct_Meaning: A performer or act, usually a singer or band, who has just one popular success.

Proverb: One good turn deserves another
Correct_Meaning: One good turn deserves another' is a proverbial expression that means, when someone does you a good turn, a good turn done in return is appropriate.

Proverb: One hand washes the other
Correct_Meaning: The proverb 'one hand washes the other' expresses the idea that mutual cooperation can help both parties.

Proverb: One swallow doesn't make a summer
Correct_Meaning: A single instance of something is just that; it doesn't indicate a trend.

Proverb: One's heart's content
Correct_Meaning: To one's (or your) heart's content means to one's complete inner satisfaction - until one's heart is content.

Proverb: Paddle your own canoe
Correct_Meaning: Act independently and decide your own fate.

Proverb: Penny saved is a penny earned - A
Correct_Meaning: The notion expressed in the proverbial saying 'A penny saved is a penny earned' is that it is as useful to save money that you already have as it is to earn more.

Proverb: Place for everything and everything in its place - A
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial notion that there should be 'a place for everything and everything in its place' is the idea that everything should have somewhere to be stored and that it should be tidily returned there when not in use.

Proverb: Plague on both your houses - A
Correct_Meaning: A frustrated curse on both sides of an argument.

Proverb: Pound of flesh
Correct_Meaning: Something which is owed that is ruthlessly required to be paid back.

Proverb: Pour oil on troubled waters
Correct_Meaning: Attempt to calm a problematic situation.

Proverb: Pride comes before a fall
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'pride comes before a fall' is a warning that haughtiness and hubris leads to failure and loss.

Proverb: Procrastination is the thief of time
Correct_Meaning: Putting off an action leads to time wasting. If something is necessary, it is best to act quickly to accomplish it.

Proverb: Proof of the pudding is in the eating - The
Correct_Meaning: To fully judge how effective something is you need to use it for its intended purpose.

Proverb: Rose by any other name would smell as sweet - A
Correct_Meaning: The saying 'A rose by any other name would smell as sweet' means that what matters is what something is, not what it is called.

Proverb: Rose is a rose is a rose
Correct_Meaning: The meaning most often attributed to 'a rose is a rose is a rose' is the notion that, when all is said and done, a thing is what it is. This is in similar vein to Shakespeare's 'a rose by any other name would smell as sweet'. However, that's not the interpretation given by the author of the phrase - see below.

Proverb: Rule of thumb
Correct_Meaning: A rule of thumb is a means of estimation made according to a rough and ready practical rule, not based on science or exact measurement.

Proverb: See a pin and pick it up, all the day you'll have good luck; see a pin and let it lie, bad luck you'll have all day
Correct_Meaning: A proverb extolling the virtue of thrift.

Proverb: Seek and you shall find
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'Seek and you shall find' means, in the Biblical sense, 'come to God and your prayers will be answered. In a wider literal sense it just means 'effort will be rewarded'.

Proverb: Seen better days
Correct_Meaning: To have been more wealthy or in better condition in former times.

Proverb: Separate the sheep from the goats
Correct_Meaning: Separate the good from the bad.

Proverb: Shebang - The whole
Correct_Meaning: All of it; the whole thing.

Proverb: Share and share alike
Correct_Meaning: To 'share and share alike' is to give equal shares to all.

Proverb: Shiver my timbers
Correct_Meaning: An oath, expressing annoyance or surprise.

Proverb: Silence is golden
Correct_Meaning: A proverbial saying, often used in circumstances where it is thought that saying nothing is preferable to speaking.

Proverb: sky's the limit
Correct_Meaning: There is no apparent limit.

Proverb: Snug as a bug in a rug
Correct_Meaning: To be 'as snug as a bug in a rug' is to be very comfortable and cosy.

Proverb: Sour grapes
Correct_Meaning: Acting meanly after a disappointment.

Proverb: Spare the rod and spoil the child
Correct_Meaning: Spare the rod and spoil the child' is the notion that children will become weak and vulnerable if not chastised, physically or otherwise, for any wrongdoing.

Proverb: Speak of the Devil
Correct_Meaning: A reference to someone who appears unexpectedly while being talked about.

Proverb: Speak softly and carry a big stick
Correct_Meaning: Speak softly and carry a big stick' is a proverbial saying advising the tactic of caution and non-aggression, backed up by the ability to carry out violent action if required.

Proverb: Standing on the shoulders of giants
Correct_Meaning: Using the understanding gained by major thinkers who have gone before in order to make intellectual progress.

Proverb: Sticks and stones may break my bones
Correct_Meaning: Sticks and stones may break my bones' is a response to an insult, implying that "You might be hurt able to hurt me by physical force but not by insults".

Proverb: Stiff upper lip
Correct_Meaning: Remain resolute and unemotional in the face of adversity, or even tragedy.

Proverb: Storm in a teacup
Correct_Meaning: A tempest in a teapot is a small or insignificant event that is over-reacted to, as if it were of considerably more consequence.

Proverb: Strike while the iron is hot
Correct_Meaning: To strike while the iron is hot is to act decisively and take an opportunity when it arises.

Proverb: Such is life
Correct_Meaning: An acceptance of the unpredictable fortunes of existence, often spoken with an air of weary resignation.

Proverb: Survival of the fittest
Correct_Meaning: The idea that species adapt and change by natural selection with the best suited mutations becoming dominant.

Proverb: Take a back seat
Correct_Meaning: To 'take a back seat' is take a subordinate or reclusive position.

Proverb: Take down a peg or two
Correct_Meaning: To 'take (or pull, or bring) down a peg (or two)' is to lower someone's high opinion of themselves.

Proverb: Take the bit between your teeth
Correct_Meaning: Take control of a situation.

Proverb: Take the cake
Correct_Meaning: Carry off the honours. Sometimes used to express incredulity; for example, "That's three goals he's missed in one game. If that don't take the cake...".

Proverb: Take the gilt off the gingerbread
Correct_Meaning: Remove an item's most attractive qualities.

Proverb: Take the Mickey
Correct_Meaning: Tease or make fun of.

Proverb: Take the upper hand
Correct_Meaning: Take a dominant position.

Proverb: Take umbrage
Correct_Meaning: To be displeased or offended by the actions of others.

Proverb: Taken aback

Proverb: The bane of my life

Proverb: The best laid schemes of mice and men

Proverb: The bitter end

Proverb: The Devil is in the details

Proverb: The ends of the earth

Proverb: The law is an ass

Proverb: The monstrous regiment of women

Proverb: The more the merrier

Proverb: The mutt's nuts

Proverb: The nth degree

Proverb: The opera ain't over till the fat lady sings

Proverb: The road less travelled

Proverb: The road to hell is paved with good intentions
Correct_Meaning: The intention to engage in good acts often fails. It points up the principle that there is no merit in good intentions unless they are acted on.

Proverb: The salt of the earth
Correct_Meaning: People who are described as 'the salt of the earth' are those who are considered to be of great worth and reliability.

Proverb: The shoemaker always wears the worst shoes
Correct_Meaning: Artisans work for the wealthy but cannot afford their own produce.

Proverb: The short end of the stick

Proverb: The writing is on the wall

Proverb: There is more than one way to kill a cat
Correct_Meaning: The proverbial saying 'There is more than one way to skin a cat' means there is more than one way of achieving an aim.

Proverb: There's one law for the rich and another law for the poor
Correct_Meaning: This proverbial saying express the opinion that the poor are treated harshly by the law whereas the rich, with their access to clever lawyers and bribes, usually escape punishment.

Proverb: Thick and thin
Correct_Meaning: Through all forms of obstacle that are put in one's way.

Proverb: thick as thieves
Correct_Meaning: Close friends with; sharing confidences.

Proverb: Thinking cap
Correct_Meaning: Take time for consideration of some question.

Proverb: Third time lucky

Proverb: Thorn in the flesh
Correct_Meaning: A persistent difficulty or annoyance.

Proverb: Though this be madness, yet there is method in it

Proverb: Three score and ten
Correct_Meaning: Three score and ten' is the nominal span of a human life. In the days that this expression was coined that span was considered to be seventy years.

Proverb: Throw in the towel
Correct_Meaning: To throw in the towel (or, to throw the towel in) is to give up, to avoid further punishment when facing certain defeat.

Proverb: Throw your hat into the ring
Correct_Meaning: Make or take up a challenge, or demonstrate one's willingness to join an enterprise.

Proverb: Till the cows come home

Proverb: Time and tide wait for no man
Correct_Meaning: No one is so powerful that they can stop the march of time.

Proverb: Tilting at windmills
Correct_Meaning: To 'tilt at windmills' is to attack imaginary enemies.

Proverb: Tissue of lies
Correct_Meaning: A story invented in order to deceive.

Proverb: To a T
Correct_Meaning: If something is said to fit 'to a T' it fits exactly; properly; precisely.

Proverb: To err is human; to forgive divine
Correct_Meaning: A proverb expressing the idea that forgiveness is a worthy response to human failings.

Proverb: To travel hopefully is a better thing than to arrive
Correct_Meaning: Hope and anticipation are often better than reality.

Proverb: Toast of the town
Correct_Meaning: A person who is widely admired.

Proverb: Toe the line
Correct_Meaning: To conform to an established standard or political programme.

Proverb: Toffee-nosed
Correct_Meaning: To be 'toffee-nosed' is to be snobbish; supercilious; stuck-up.

Correct_Meaning: Conceited; having a too high opinion of oneself.

Correct_Meaning: Excess may do you harm.

Proverb: Top dog
Correct_Meaning: One who is dominant or victorious.

Proverb: Touch and go

Proverb: Touch wood

Proverb: Tower of strength
Correct_Meaning: Someone who can be relied on to provide support and comfort.

Proverb: True blue
Correct_Meaning: Loyal and unwavering in one's opinions or support for a cause.

Proverb: Truth will out
Correct_Meaning: The truth will become known eventually.

Proverb: Turkeys voting for Christmas

Proverb: Turn a blind eye
Correct_Meaning: To turn a blind eye is to knowingly refuse to acknowledge something which you know to be real.

Proverb: Turn the tables
Correct_Meaning: Reverse the positions of adversaries. The phrases is often used when the weaker position subsequently becomes dominant.

Proverb: Turn up trumps
Correct_Meaning: To turn out well or successfully.

Proverb: Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown
Correct_Meaning: The expression 'uneasy lies the head that wears a crown' means that a person with great power, such as a king, is constantly apprehensive.

Proverb: Up a blind alley
Correct_Meaning: Following a course of action that leads to no good outcome.

Proverb: Up a gum tree

Proverb: Up in arms
Correct_Meaning: Roused; incensed.

Proverb: Up the creek without a paddle
Correct_Meaning: In an awkward situation or unpleasant predicament.

Proverb: Up the duff

Proverb: Up the wooden hill to Bedfordshire

Proverb: Up to snuff
Correct_Meaning: Initially, the phrase meant 'sharp and in the know'; more recently, 'up to the required standard'.

Proverb: Upper crust
Correct_Meaning: Aristocratic; society superior.

Proverb: Up the ante

Proverb: Using a sledgehammer to crack a nut
Correct_Meaning: To use 'a sledgehammer to crack a nut' means to use disproportionate force or expense to overcome a minor problem.

Proverb: Vicious circle
Correct_Meaning: A self-perpetuating process which returns to its starting point with no improvement from when it was begun.

Proverb: Warts and all
Correct_Meaning: Warts and all' means the whole thing; not concealing the less attractive parts.

Proverb: Wax lyrical
Correct_Meaning: Speak niin an increasingly enthusiastic and poetic manner.

Proverb: Don’t put off until tomorrow what you can do today
Correct_Meaning: If you can do something today, do it. Don’t wait until tomorrow; don’t procrastinate.

Proverb: The enemy of my enemy is my friend
Correct_Meaning: If someone whom I don’t like doesn’t like someone else whom I don’t like, we can act like friends and unite against the other person (common in war)

Proverb: The pen is mightier than the sword
Correct_Meaning: If you’re trying to convince someone of something, words and ideas are stronger than using physical force (common in politics)

Proverb: There is no time like the present
Correct_Meaning: Don’t wait to do something. Do it now.

Proverb: The squeaky wheel gets the grease
Correct_Meaning: The person who complains in a situation is more likely to get something.

Proverb: A fool and his money are soon parted.
Correct_Meaning: Fools lose money because of their foolish conduct.

Proverb: After victory, tighten your helmet chord.
Correct_Meaning: There is no room for complacency. Get down to work after a victory. Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon, calls it Day 0 mentality.

Proverb: A good listener is a silent flatterer.
Correct_Meaning: Human beings have an innate desire to be listened, but only few are good listeners. So, if you listen to someone attentively, you’ll flatter them.

Proverb: A goose quill is more dangerous than a lion’s claw.
Correct_Meaning: Foul, inconsiderate words can cause more pain than a physical attack.

Proverb: One law for the rich and another for the poor.
Correct_Meaning: The law is same for both, but the rich, through their abundant resources, can get favourable decisions by influencing decision makers, hiring the best lawyers, and delaying the case if it suits them, among several measures at their command.

Proverb: Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day; teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.

Proverb: Hope for the best and prepare for the worst.
Correct_Meaning: One should be positive, but at the same time be ready to face hardships.

Proverb: History repeats itself.

Proverb: A hedge between keeps friendship green.
Correct_Meaning: Giving enough space to each other help maintain a good relationship.

Proverb: Health is better than wealth.
Correct_Meaning: Physical well-being is more important than financial prosperity.

Proverb: He laughs best who laughs last.
Correct_Meaning: People who laugh first may have others laugh at them in the end.

Proverb: Haste makes waste.
Correct_Meaning: Too much of a hurry leads to mistakes and loss of productivity.

Proverb: The hand that rocks the cradle rules the world.
Correct_Meaning: Mothers who care for their children are creating the next generation of men.

Proverb: Half a loaf is better than no bread.
Correct_Meaning: One should be thankful for whatever one gets, considering one may otherwise get nothing.

Proverb: Great oaks from little acorns grow.

Proverb: Grapes are sour.
Correct_Meaning: When people cannot get what they desire, they save face by pretending they never wanted it.

Proverb: A good name is sooner lost than won.
Correct_Meaning: A reputation takes long to build, but can be quickly destroyed.

Proverb: A good husband makes a good wife.
Correct_Meaning: One who treats others well will be treated well in return.

Proverb: God tempers the wind to the shorn lamb.
Correct_Meaning: Heaven is more kind to the weak.

Proverb: A friend in need is a friend indeed.
Correct_Meaning: True friends are those who help in difficult times.

Proverb: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
Correct_Meaning: Spread your risks widely and wisely.

Correct_Meaning: Always do things in the right order.

Correct_Meaning: One should not be arrogant.

Correct_Meaning: It is best to confine shameful family matters to the home.

Proverb: East or west, home is best.
Correct_Meaning: Wherever one may travel, the happiest place is one's abode.

Proverb: Easy come, easy go.
Correct_Meaning: What is acquired without effort especially money is likely to be lost.

Proverb: Every cloud has a silver lining.
Correct_Meaning: There is hope even in difficult situations.

Proverb: Fortune favors the bold.
Correct_Meaning: Success comes to those who have the courage to try.

Proverb: Once bitten, twice shy.

Proverb: One good turn deserves another.
Correct_Meaning: If someone has been kind to you, then you should return the kindness.

Proverb: One is never too old to learn.
Correct_Meaning: Whatever our age and however much we know, we can still increase our knowledge.

Proverb: One man's meat is another man's poison.

Proverb: One must draw the line somewhere.
Correct_Meaning: There is a definite limit beyond which one decides not to go.

Proverb: One swallow does not make a summer.

Proverb: Out of sight out of mind.

Proverb: The pen is mightier than the sword.
Correct_Meaning: The written word has more power to cause change than physical force.

Proverb: Poverty is no sin.

Proverb: Respect is greater from a distance.

Proverb: A stitch in time saves nine.

Proverb: The strength of the chain is in the weakest link.

Proverb: Strike while the iron is hot.

Proverb: The tailor makes the man.
Correct_Meaning: A person can appear attractive in good clothes.

Proverb: Take care of the pennies and the pounds will take care of themselves.
Correct_Meaning: Savings in small amounts will eventually lead to a large total.

Proverb: There are as good fish in the sea as ever came out of it.
Correct_Meaning: If an opportunity is missed, there will be plenty more.

Proverb: Talk of the devil and the devil appears.
Correct_Meaning: This is said in jest when a person we have been talking about meets us.

Proverb: There's many a slip between the cup and the lip.

Proverb: There is no rose without a thorn.

Proverb: A thing of beauty is a joy forever.

Proverb: Uneasy lies the head that wears the crown.

Proverb: Variety is the spice of life.
Correct_Meaning: Experiencing different things makes living interesting and prevents boredom.

Proverb: Wake not a sleeping lion.
Correct_Meaning: It is wise not to disturb things at times lest you invite trouble.

Proverb: Walls have ears.

Proverb: Waste not, want not.
Correct_Meaning: If one is careful with things especially money, one will not lack them when needed.

Proverb: Water is a boon in the desert, but the drowning man curses it.
Correct_Meaning: There is too little of what we want and too much of what we don't want.

Proverb: Well begun is half done.

Proverb: When in Rome do as the Romans do.

Proverb: When one door shuts another opens.

Proverb: When the cat is away the mice will play.

Proverb: Where there's a will there's a way.

Proverb: The wish is father to the thought.

Proverb: You cannot have your cake and eat it.
Correct_Meaning: You cannot have everything because a choice has to be made between alternatives.

Proverb: You can take a horse to the water, but you cannot make him drink.
Correct_Meaning: You cannot help an unwilling person beyond a certain point.

Proverb: You scratch my back and I'll scratch yours.
Correct_Meaning: You do me a favor and I will reciprocate.

Proverb: Beauty is but skin deep.
Correct_Meaning: Do not judge solely by looks because appearances are deceptive.

Proverb: Every ass likes to hear himself bray.
Correct_Meaning: Foolish people talk a lot.

Proverb: Nothing venture, nothing gain.
Correct_Meaning: Without risks, there are no rewards.

Proverb: You can lead a horse to the water, but you can’t make him drink it
Correct_Meaning: You can advise someone or show them how to do something, but you can’t force them to accept or mak them do it.

Proverb: A bird in hand is worth two in the bush
Correct_Meaning: Certainty of having something in hand is better than mere probability of having even more things.

Proverb: A drowning man will clutch a straw
Correct_Meaning: When someone is in a difficult situation, s/he will take any available opportunity to come out of it.

Proverb: A happy heart is better than a full purse
Correct_Meaning: What’s the use of money if you’re unhappy despite loads of it? Happiness is better than plenty.

Proverb: All is fair in love and war
Correct_Meaning: One can break the rules of fair play under extenuating circumstances.

Proverb: All is well that ends well
Correct_Meaning: As long as the outcome is good, problems on the way don’t matter.

Proverb: All lay loads on a willing horse
Correct_Meaning: A person who says ‘yes’, even if hesitatingly, to any work given to him will soon find himself overloaded with work.

Proverb: Among the blind, one-eyed man is king
Correct_Meaning: An incapable person can gain powerful position if others in the fray are even more incapable.

Proverb: An army of sheep led by a lion would defeat an army of lions led by a sheep
Correct_Meaning: This proverb exemplifies importance of leadership. A strong army (lions) led by a weak leader (sheep) can lose to a weak army (sheep) led by a strong leader (lion).

Proverb: An empty vessel makes much noise
Correct_Meaning: Fools and persons with shallow knowledge often talk a lot.

Proverb: An hour in the morning is worth two in the evening
Correct_Meaning: People are generally more productive in the morning: first, they’re fresh after night’s sleep; second, there are fewer distractions in the morning.

Proverb: A tree is known by its fruit
Correct_Meaning: Like a tree is known by the fruit it bears, people are known by their character and actions (and not by their appearance)

Proverb: Begin to weave and God will give the thread
Correct_Meaning: When taking up a task that has no playbook to follow, we plan a lot and think a lot but don’t act. In such pursuits, you can’t foresee everything in advance and lot of assumptions will come to naught.

Proverb: Best things in life are free
Correct_Meaning: Most valuable things are often free.

Proverb: Cowards die many times before their death
Correct_Meaning: Cowards suffer the feared effects of death many times in their lives.

Proverb: Do as you would be done by
Correct_Meaning: Treat others like the way you would like to be treated.

Proverb: Doctors make the worst patients
Correct_Meaning: It’s difficult to advice a person on a matter in which he is an expert.

Proverb: Don’t carry coals to Newcastle
Correct_Meaning: In the past, Newcastle was known for its coal mines. Coal was mined here and taken to other parts of England. So, if you carry coal to Newcastle, you’re doing unnecessary work.

Proverb: Don’t cross the bridge till you come to it
Correct_Meaning: Deal with a situation when it happens and not unnecessarily worry about it in advance.

Proverb: Don’t kill the goose that lays golden eggs
Correct_Meaning: If you kill a goose that lays golden eggs, you destroy something that makes lot of money for you.

Proverb: Don’t think there are no crocodiles because the water is calm
Correct_Meaning: Everything calm and peaceful doesn’t mean there are no dangers around.

Proverb: Don’t throw the baby with the bathwater
Correct_Meaning: Don’t discard something valuable while getting rid of something worthless.

Proverb: Empty bags can’t stand upright
Correct_Meaning: A poor or hungry person cannot discharge his duties well.

Proverb: Every horse thinks its own pack is heaviest
Correct_Meaning: We think that we work the hardest. This is also called responsibility bias: People tend to overvalue their own contributions and undervalue contributions of others.

Proverb: Every tub must stand on its own bottom
Correct_Meaning: We can’t hide incompetency behind teamwork. Everyone has to justify their expense.

Proverb: Fall seven times; stand up eight.
Correct_Meaning: Be resilient and try despite failures. That’s how you succeed.

Proverb: Faults are thick where love is thin
Correct_Meaning: If the love is shallow, people will find faults in each other.

Proverb: Flattery, like perfume, should be smelled but not swallowed
Correct_Meaning: Enjoy the flattery you receive, but don’t believe it because people often flatter to meet their own selfish interests.

Proverb: For want of a nail the shoe is lost, for want of a shoe the horse is lost, for want of a horse the rider is lost
Correct_Meaning: in insignificant nail resulted in the loss of the rider. Small things can have huge implications. So, don’t ignore nuances and minute details. They’re the ones that stand people out.

Proverb: If you buy cheaply, you pay dearly
Correct_Meaning: Something cheap will be of suspect quality and will trouble you later in the form of higher maintenance and/or poor performance.

Proverb: If you can’t beat them, join them

Proverb: If you want peace, prepare for war

Proverb: Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery
Correct_Meaning: Words of flattery may not be sincere. But action (imitation) is sincere. Who wouldn’t be flattered if someone imitates them in some way?

Proverb: It is easy to find a thousand soldiers, but hard to find a good general
Correct_Meaning: Leaders are not easy to find. Retain them at whatever price it takes if you’ve them.

Proverb: It takes two to make a quarrel
Correct_Meaning: Without involvement of at least two persons, a quarrel won’t happen. So, if one of the two persons decide, a quarrel won’t happen.

Proverb: Kind words will unlock an iron door
Correct_Meaning: If you talk politely, people are more amenable to your suggestions and ask.

Proverb: Kings have long arms
